blogs.title: Instead of Making Predictions, This AI Learns the Rules First
blogs.description: This post explains the core idea behind FeatLLM in plain language: using a large language model as a feature engineer rather than as a direct predictor. It would show how the model reads a small number of examples, writes human-like decision rules, turns those rules into new binary features, and then lets a simple classifier make the final prediction. The post would focus on why this is a clever shift from 'LLM as black box' to 'LLM as rule maker.'

blogs.title: Why LLMs Struggle With Tables—and How FeatLLM Gets Around It
blogs.description: This post would focus on the practical limitations of existing LLM-based tabular methods, such as long prompts, per-sample inference cost, and the need for fine-tuning. It would then explain how FeatLLM avoids these bottlenecks by querying the LLM only during feature creation, not at prediction time. The article would be especially useful for readers interested in deployment, scalability, and cost.

blogs.title: Few Examples, Strong Results: How FeatLLM Boosts Low-Data Machine Learning
blogs.description: This post would center on the paper's few-shot learning results and why they matter. It would explain how FeatLLM performs well even when only a handful of labeled examples are available, often beating standard tabular models and other LLM-based baselines. The blog would translate the benchmark findings into real-world terms for industries like healthcare, finance, and science, where labeled data can be scarce and expensive.

blogs.title: From Natural Language Rules to Machine Learning Features
blogs.description: This post would dive into the mechanics of the system: prompt design, two-step reasoning, rule extraction, code generation, and feature transformation. It would explain how FeatLLM turns natural-language insights like 'older age increases risk' into structured signals a simple model can use. The emphasis would be on making the method understandable to technical readers who want to know how the pipeline actually works.

blogs.title: Can AI Be a Better Feature Engineer Than Humans?
blogs.description: This post would explore the broader implications of the paper, including interpretability, robustness, and the promise of LLMs as knowledge-driven assistants for structured data. It would discuss the evidence that many generated rules are genuinely informative, how ensembling helps filter bad rules, and where the approach could still fail due to bias or spurious correlations. The article would frame FeatLLM as part of a bigger shift in how AI might support data science workflows.
